briefs.source_chain: Strong US/Eurozone flash PMIs plus hawkish UN rhetoric (Iran deal further off, no Russia-sanctions consensus) mean the market was underpricing terminal Fed funds, therefore yields spiked (weak-demand 5Y auction with 3.20bp tail, 5Y breaks 5% since 2007) and oil broke back above $100 on Iran escalation, therefore JPM stays Tactically Cautious/Neutral running +Tech(NDX)/-RTY, bullish only on lower oil/yields, bearish only on a broken consumer or an AI capex cut.
briefs.brief_chain: Same chain: stronger PMIs + UN rhetoric drove yields higher on underpriced terminal Fed funds, 5Y broke 5% on a weak 3.20bp-tail auction, hot PMI input costs raised hike-timing risk, oil broke $100 on Iran escalation, JPM stays Tactically Cautious/Neutral (+Tech vs -RTY), bullish only on lower oil/yields, bearish on a broken consumer or AI capex cut.

briefs.source_chain: A historic bond selloff (10Y worst since Liberation Day, 5Y above 5% since 2007) coincides with high oil/CPI, but stable breakevens and range-bound term premium rule out an inflation or fiscal story, therefore the move is about policy rates and a rising neutral rate (Warsh: growth/capital-competition-as-AI-capex/geopolitics; Raskin's plausible-but-elevated neutral-rate band is now nearly reached), amplified by strong PMIs, GDPNow at 5.08%, ~30% Q3 EPS growth and positioning.
briefs.brief_chain: Same chain: bond selloff occurs alongside high oil/CPI, DB argues via stable breakevens and flat term premium that it isn't an inflation story, attributes the move to real yields/policy rates and a higher neutral rate (Warsh's three drivers, Raskin's band now nearly reached), with PMIs/GDPNow/earnings growth/positioning as amplifiers.

briefs.source_chain: Beat-expectation US/Eurozone flash PMIs plus an oil rebound (Iran-deal doubts) drove a hawkish repricing (Fed October-hike odds 53%→69%→71% this morning; ECB 48%→66%), pushing the 10Y to a post-2007 high (+15.2bp, biggest move since Liberation Day) and the 5Y above 5% since 2007 on a weak tailed 5Y auction, with European yields and the Franco-German spread also at multi-year wides, therefore equities fell broadly (S&P -0.75%, worst in a month) except energy.
briefs.brief_chain: Same chain, same figures and sequence, with one date label swapped: 'rose from 53% Tuesday to 69% by Thursday's close, with this morning's futures pricing 71%' where the source's 69% figure is 'last night's close' (i.e. the prior day, not 'Thursday').

distortions.what: Brief labels the 69% Fed October-hike print as reached 'by Thursday's close'; the source only supports 69% by 'last night's close' (the day before this morning-of report), with 71% being 'this morning' — the brief effectively invents an extra day in the timeline.
distortions.would_the_trade_change: No — the hawkish-repricing direction, magnitude, and every downstream figure (yields, spreads, equity moves) are unaffected by which calendar day is named for the intermediate print.

briefs.source_chain: Agentic-AI anticipation drove dispersion (big tech bid to Nasdaq record, banks battered on GS's AI-disruption call, dragging the Dow while SPX finished flat), oil whipsawed on a chain of Iran-Hormuz headlines before closing down (WTI -3.5%) on the final 'momentum for a deal / reopening Hormuz' headline even as Trump separately ruled out a deal before the Midterms, Trump floated a diesel export ban, Treasury yields finished flat with rate-hike odds unmoved despite falling inflation expectations (Goldman's 'weird bit'), hyperscaler credit widened a fourth day, both LO and HF desks were net sellers on subdued volume, and breadth (new lows > new highs) drew a 1999/1929 comparison from CNBC for a specific rally-to-highs pattern.
briefs.brief_chain: Same big-tech-vs-banks dispersion and causes; oil narrative compressed to reversal on the Fars denial and Saudi pipeline hopes, then straight to 'WTI down 3.5% after Trump called his Iran meeting very good' — skipping the intervening optimism-fade bounce and the second plunge (on the later Hormuz-flow headlines) that the -3.5% print actually followed; yields-flat is described as itself Goldman's 'weird bit' rather than the unmoved rate-hike odds; the six-straight-day new-lows-over-new-highs stat is presented as the same thing CNBC compared to 1999/1929, when CNBC's comparison was to a narrower single-day pattern (S&P near highs with new lows surging/new highs tumbling).

distortions.what: Brief attributes the final WTI -3.5% print directly to Trump's 'very good meeting' comment, but the source's causal chain has that comment followed by a bounce-back and a second plunge driven by separate 'momentum for a deal / reopening Hormuz' headlines, which is what the -3.5% figure actually follows.
distortions.would_the_trade_change: No — oil closed lower on Iran-related headline chop either way; no stance, level call, or instrument changes from naming the wrong link in a multi-leg intraday chain.

distortions.what: Brief says Goldman called 'yields ended flat... the weird bit'; the source attributes 'the weird bit' to rate-hike odds going nowhere despite falling inflation expectations, a related but distinct observation from yields being flat.
distortions.would_the_trade_change: No — both describe the same disconnect (falling inflation expectations not showing up in rates pricing); no directional or trade implication differs.

distortions.what: Brief implies CNBC's 1999/1929 comparison applies to the six-straight-day new-lows-over-new-highs statistic; the source's CNBC quote instead compares a narrower one-day pattern (S&P rallying to near record highs while new lows surge and new highs tumble) to 1999 and 1929.
distortions.would_the_trade_change: No — the underlying warning (deteriorating breadth alongside index strength, historically rare and ominous) is preserved; conflating the two breadth stats doesn't change any call.
